title: Three times of prayer
hook: Shia usually combine the five prayers into three times of day, which Sunni schools allow in certain cases

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turbah, the small tablet of clay, and your line: forehead on earth. When did you last put your hands on bare ground, and what did it feel like under them? Day one thousand two hundred two.

A family in Detroit finishes lunch, and someone lays out the prayer mats. They pray the noon prayer, stand quietly for a moment, and then pray the afternoon prayer straight after it. That evening it happens again: sunset, then night, one after the other. Their neighbor down the street, who also prays five times a day, waits for the afternoon prayer until the shadows have grown long. Same Qur'an, same five prayers, same direction. Two different clocks. Neither family is cutting corners. Each is following a school, and each school can show you its reasons. Today is about how five prayers can sit in three times of day.
screen: `NOON, THEN AFTERNOON, BACK TO BACK.` → `A NEIGHBOR WAITS FOR THE SHADOWS.` → `FIVE PRAYERS, TWO CLOCKS.`

segments.voice: Start with what everyone shares. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours. That verse is common ground: the prayers have times. The question is how wide those times are. Next, the verse the schools read differently. In surah seventeen, the Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to establish prayer from the sun's decline until the dark of night, and the recitation at dawn. Some readers hear three moments in that verse: the decline of the sun, the dark of night, and dawn. Then, a report. In Sahih Muslim, Ibn Abbas says the Prophet prayed noon and afternoon together, and sunset and night together, in Medina, with no fear and no rain. Asked why, Ibn Abbas said he wanted no hardship for his community. Ja'fari scholars, followed by Twelver Shia, read the verse and the report together: noon and afternoon share one stretch of time, and so do sunset and night. Praying each at its own moment is good, they teach, and joining them is permitted any day. So a Shia family can pray the five in three sittings: dawn, midday, evening. Last, the Sunni schools. They know the same report, and they also allow joining, called jam', but for set reasons. Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali scholars allow it on a journey, and some for heavy rain or illness. Hanafi scholars allow it on pilgrimage, at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Otherwise, each prayer is prayed in its own time. Two readings of the same texts: one widens the time, the other keeps each prayer in its own.
screen: `COMMON GROUND: PRAYER HAS FIXED HOURS.` · `ONE VERSE, READ AS THREE MOMENTS.` · `IBN ABBAS: JOINED, IN MEDINA, NO RAIN.` · `SUNNI SCHOOLS: JOIN FOR SET REASONS.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice the times you pray, or the times you stop. Think back over yesterday. When did your day pause? Maybe at dawn, maybe at lunch, maybe at a red light, maybe only at night. Count the pauses on your fingers. If you pray, notice which prayers you pray in their own moment and which you gather together, and where your school draws that line. If you don't, notice where your day already has its natural stops, the places a prayer could sit. No judging, just counting. The bell holds the time.
Three times of prayer. In Ja'fari practice, the five prayers prayed in three sittings; in Sunni schools, joining allowed on a journey and for certain other needs. Today's word.

Your line: five in three. Today, when you hear a call to prayer or see someone pray, remember the clock might differ while the five stay the same. Tomorrow, a school from the mountains of Yemen. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: Twelver Shia follow Ja'fari law, which lets noon and afternoon, and sunset and night, be prayed together, so the five prayers are often prayed in three sittings; Sunni schools join prayers for set reasons such as travel, rain, or the pilgrimage.

fork.setup: you're with Ibn Abbas. someone asks why the Prophet joined noon and afternoon in Medina, with no journey, no fear, no rain. what does he answer?
options: he wanted no hardship for his community.
fork.reveal: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet wanted no hardship for his community. the schools then read that report in different ways.

original.note: Arabic: gathering, joining; in law, praying two prayers together in one time.

trapdoor: what you thought: some Muslims pray five times a day and some pray three.
what it means: all pray five; the schools differ on how wide each prayer's time is and when two may be joined.
what a scholar hears: al-jam' bayna al-salatayn, Ibn Abbas's report in Sahih Muslim, and the long reading of surah 17:78.

sources.quoted: Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 705 (Ibn Abbas: joining in Medina without fear or rain)

notes: Editor: cut the teach's closing 'nobody here is skipping a prayer', which repeated the hook's 'neither family is cutting corners'.
Qur'an 17:78 paraphrased; the reading of it as three times (decline of the sun, dark of night, dawn) is presented as how 'some readers' hear it: confirm fair to Ja'fari usage.
Sahih Muslim 705: confirm number and paraphrase (no fear and no rain; reason: no hardship for his community). Some versions say 'no fear and no travel'.
Ja'fari position (shared time for paired prayers; separating preferred, joining permitted without cause): confirm framing.
Sunni positions: Shafi'i/Maliki/Hanbali allow joining on travel and some for rain or illness (Hanbali); Hanafi only at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Confirm summary.
Detroit family scene is illustrative, not a reported case.
